newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia warlords rush to disarm before deadline.
newsitem.headline: Liberia warlords rush to disarm before deadline.

text.p: Liberia's warlords are rushing to disarm their fighters by Friday's deadline under a peace deal targeting elections in May, West African peacekeepers and U.N. officials say.
General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force, says any fighters found to be armed after the deadline will be treated as "criminals".
"We have received more weapons per day in the last four days than we did for over one month," Kent Page, a U.N. spokesman, told Reuters on Monday.

The slow pace of demobilisation and the poor quality of weapons surrendered since the disarmament exercise began on November 22 drew fire in mid-January from Liberia's West African neighbours, who brokered the peace deal.
Page said 12,231 fighters had demobilised by Saturday.
The United Nations, which is overseeing the demobilisation, puts the number of fighters at 60,000, saying this was based on figures provided by the factions themselves in 1994.
The factions say the number is much lower, following deaths and demobilisation since 1994. The National Disarmament and Demobilisation Commission says there are 23,800 fighters.

U.N. officials and peacekeepers say hundreds of fighters are disarming. The disarmament site on Randall Street in Monrovia was a hive of activity on Monday, with fighters coming in from outlying districts to surrender their arms to peacekeepers or U.N. monitors.
Rival faction leaders, ranging from Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war in 1989, to his arch-foe Roosevelt Johnson, say they will disarm their men by the deadline.
"The Liberia Peace Council is dissolved as of January 31 and all former combattants bearing arms this date will be doing so on their own accord," the council's leader, George Boley, said.
He estimated half his 4,650 fighters had so far disarmed.
Johnson, the man at the centre of last year's flare-up in the capital Monrovia, said on Sunday in Sierra Leone's capital Freetown that 5,000 of his fighters had disarmed.

Johnson heads the ethnic krahn wing of the ULIMO group, set up to block Taylor's bid for power in Liberia. He said the rest of his 15,000-strong force had no weapons or would disarm once peacekeepers deployed in the areas they controlled.
Taylor, who heads the largest faction, demobilised a 1,500-man artillery battalion on Saturday at his Gbarnga headquarters and says he too will meet the deadline.
But on Tuesday, Taylor plans to take time off to marry his long-standing girl-friend Juwel Howard, who is deputy governor at Liberia's Central Bank, his supporters say.
They said the wedding was switched from Monrovia to Gbarnga for security reasons. Some said a hit squad planned to assassinate Taylor on his wedding day.
The peace plan, signed in Nigeria's capital Abuja in August, envisages disarmament and elections. West African leaders have threatened sanctions against any warlord derailing the process.

Malu on Sunday threatened to execute peacekeepers collaborating with fighters, many of whom have been handing in ECOMOG weapons. "We will be very ruthless against anyone found bearing arms at that time," he said, referring to the deadline.
Taylor and his fellow interim ruling council vice-chairman Alhaji Kromah, who heads the ethnic mandingo wing of ULIMO, have both announced their intention to stand in the May elections.
Sometime rivals, they united against Johnson in fighting which held Monrovia hostage and killed hundreds of people in April and May, until West African peacekeepers restored order.
Johnson says he plans to go into business: "I am not going to contest either presidential or parliamentary elections."
Freed American slaves founded Liberia in 1847. The civil war has killed well over 150,000 people.
